processing: A half-baked, half-pan-fired green tea made from tender, downy leaf.
harvest_season: Mainly spring: Shangnan's cool climate means picking centres on spring tea, and little summer tea is made.
appearance_dry: Fine, tender leaf with plenty of visible down.
appearance_liquor: A clear, pale yellow-green is typical of Shangnan greens.
appearance_wet: Tender leaf in a bright yellow-green.
taste_profile: Fresh and mellow, with a soft young-chestnut aroma rather than a loud one.

brewing.notes: These are general settings for a downy green. Slightly warmer water brings out the chestnut note, but stop short of boiling.

vintage_note: It is sold as the current year's spring tea, as usual for fine Chinese greens, and is best within about a year. It is a named style within Shangnan tea, so a packet may carry both names.
description:
Shangnan Quanming is the best-known named tea of Shangnan county in the Qinling area of southeastern Shaanxi, a very northerly place to grow tea at all.

It is a half-baked, half-pan-fired green made from fine young leaf, which keeps plenty of down and gives a bright yellow-green leaf after brewing.

The point of the tea is its chestnut note, here gentle and elegant rather than toasty, over a fresh, mellow taste. A little patience and water just below 85°C will show it best.

Buy the current spring tea, ask for the maker, and compare it with a broader Shangnan tea to see what the finer leaf adds.
history:
The tea first went by the plain name Maojian, then Quanshuiqing. On 14 June 1987, the China Tea Research Institute reviewed it, described its fine downy leaf and young-chestnut aroma, and suggested the present name, Shangnan Quanming.

Its story is tied to Shangnan's young tea industry, which took off only after tea was introduced successfully around 1970.
